--- title: "Ginko Trees" author: "DK" date: "2026-10-11" categories: [relationships] --- 참으로 오랜만이었네. 천 년을 사는 은행나무는 몇십 년에 한 번씩 봐도 되지만, 백 년도 못 사는 사람은 몇 년에 한 번이라도 보고 사는 게 친척 아니겠나. 반가웠고 잘 살아줘서 고맙네. 어디에 얼마나 멀리 살아도 늘 기억하고 추억하며 열심히 살고 건강하세. ![](images/20261013_111452~2.jpg) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ > *It really had been such a long time!* > > *The ginkgo tree, which lives a thousand years, can be seen once every few decades and still be fine.* > > *But people, who don’t even live a hundred years, should see each other at least once every few years—that’s what being relatives is all about.* > > *It was so good to see you, and thank you for living well.* > > *No matter where we live or how far apart we may be, let’s remember each other, cherish our memories, keep working hard, and stay healthy.* > > — **Uncle H, October 2026** --- In life, we are blessed with two families: the family we are born into, and the family we join through marriage. When I married Sister K, my world expanded to include her extended family—a network that included eight aunts and two uncles. Her older uncle was a few years senior to her father, while her younger uncle was nearly twenty years younger, making him much closer to our own age. Recently, we made arrangements to visit this younger uncle, Uncle H, and his new wife. We had initially planned for a simple dinner, but Uncle H suggested something far better: > *"Instead of just coming for dinner, come earlier and let me show you around town."* His invitation demonstrated the wisdom of someone who understands how relationships work in life. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- Our walk took us along a street lined with ginkgo trees, now transformed into a pedestrian-only avenue The walk became both nostalgic and futuristic. As we walked beneath their canopy, Uncle H looked up at the branches and shared a piece of his history. Some sixty years ago, as a junior high student, he and his classmates were given time off from school to plant those very trees, which were about ten years old at the time. I asked with a touch of levity if that mandatory planting felt like forced labor in a work camp. He replied, > *"No, we worked with pride. We were born here, and we were beautifying our own town."* ![](images/20261011_155129.jpg) As we walked, a group coming from the opposite direction stopped to exchange warm greetings. Uncle H welcomed them like old friends. It turned out his friend was a four-term 국회의원 *Gukhoe-uiwon*—a Member of the National Assembly. A short distance later, he waved to the chair of the festival music program who had attended the same school he did. Waves of friends, neighbors, and acquaintances continued to pass by—a fruit of living in the same town for over seventy years. ![](images/20261011_161519.jpg) Eventually, he directed our walk toward the river, where sections of carefully curated flowers bloomed along the banks. There, by the water, his attention shifted from the past to our future. He offered us counsel drawn from his own life, ranging from financial wisdom to the nuances of family relations. He spoke not in a lecturing tone, but with the quiet, concern of a family member, 작은아버지 (*Jageun-abeoji)*—a "little father." By the time we turned back, we were a few minutes late for dinner. But as we climbed up to the fourth-floor living area overlooking the Onyang Market 온양시장 area, we understood why we had taken that three-hour detour. --- His wife of six years had spent hours—perhaps days—preparing a feast fit for honored guests. I had rarely seen so many dishes presented in a single sitting, each one prepared with care and love. This was my first time meeting 작은엄마, connected to her only through the bonds of marriage. Yet she honored us out of her devotion and commitment to the family. I came away from that visit both enriched and resolved—deeply grateful for the family I gained through marriage, and inspired by a quiet resolve to live more like Uncle H. ![](images/1791714680376.jpg)
